newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New American U.N. envoy Richardson takes up post.
newsitem.headline: New American U.N. envoy Richardson takes up post.

text.p: The new United States U.N. ambassador, Bill Richardson, presented his credentials on Tuesday to Secretary-General Kofi Annan and affirmed Washington's commitment to the ideals of the United Nations.

"On behalf of President Bill Clinton, on behalf of Secretary (of State Madeleine) Albright, it is an honour for me to present my credentials to you," he told Annan, who took over as secretary-general on Jan. 1.

"Let me state that the United States reaffirms its very strong commitment to the Charter of the United Nations, to the goals of the United Nations -- international peace and security, human rights, economic and social development," Richardson said.

Commending Annan "for the excellent start that you have made here at the United Nations," the 49-year-old former Democratic congressman from New Mexico also stressed the importance the United States attached to the world organisation.

Shortly afterwards, Richardson, a former congressman from New Mexico, met China's U.N. delegation, the first of many he will visit. True to form, he evidently told a joke which caused Ambassador Qin Huasun to break out in loud laughter.

Applying a politician's touch he toured the U.N. cafeteria, shaking hands and introducing himself to startled but pleased U.N. employees, unused to such a gesture from American envoys or those from any other country. "We care about all U.N. employees, not just the ambassadors and the high-level people," he said.
"I went into the cafeteria to shake hands with all employees to symbolise that there is a new era between the United States and United Nations."
Richardson, who gained a reputation as a diplomatic trouble-shooter while still a congressman, succeeds Madeleine Albright, now the Secretary of State.
Annan, who visited the White House and the U.S. Congress last month, asked Richardson to convey his best wishes to President Clinton.
"The United Nations needs U.S. leadership, but the U.S. also needs the United Nations," he said, sounding an oft-repeated theme.

"We look forward to working with you and the (U.S.) administration and ensuring that the U.S. is firmly back in the fold, with the question of arrears behind us as we move ahead in strengthening and reshaping this organisation. Welcome aboard !"
Annan was alluding to the twin issues of U.N. reform, which Washington has long demanded, and U.S. payment of long-standing U.N. arrears.

The United States has cited the slow pace of U.N. reform, and resulting disenchantment among members of the Republican-dominated Congress, as the main reason for vetoing the re-election of Annan's predecessor, Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali of Egypt.

The United States is assessed 25 percent of the organisation's annual regular budget of about $1.3 billion and more than 31 percent of its peacekeeping costs and owes well over $1 billion in unpaid contributions. The Clinton administration hopes to appropriate $100 million this year, with the remainder to be approved but held until 1999.
Richardson travelled to North Korea last November to win the release of a young American detained on espionage changes.
Shortly afterwards, he flew to Sudan to help free three Red Cross workers held hostage by a rebel leader.
In 1995 he met Iraqi President Saddam Hussein to negotiate the release of two American engineers who had strayed over the border from Kuwait.

Richardson speaks grew up mostly in Mexico City, where his father was a bank executive. He is of American and Mexican ancestry and he immediately used his flawless Spanish in comments to Latin American reporters.
"I had a great reception. It will be an exciting four years," he told Reuters.

"Our message is reform, pay our arrears and go to the American people, talking about the importance of the United Nations. The United Nations advances American interests. That's a big plus for the American people," he said.
